description_full: TORM plc, a shipping company, owns and operates a fleet of product tankers in the United Kingdom and internationally. It operates in two segments, Tanker and Marine Engineering. The Tanker segment transports refined oil products, such as gasoline, jet fuel, diesel, naphtha, and gas oil, as well as dirty petroleum products, such as residual fuels and crude oil. The Marine Engineering segment engages in developing and producing advanced and green marine equipment. TORM plc was founded in 1889 and is based in London, the United Kingdom.

financial_summary: TORM plc is a mid-cap energy business with a $3.8B market cap on $1.3B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at -2% over the past three years, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome. Operating margins are contracting by -5.0pp, the first warning that competitive pressure is eroding the franchise.
Returns on capital run at 26% against a 8% cost of capital — a 17-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $190M in free cash flow — roughly 14 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.74× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.0× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 4.8×.

Management returns a meaningful 5.2% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 20% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 2.4× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Geopolitical supply shocks — wars, sanctions, and OPEC decisions create volatility that no hedging programme can fully neutralise.
